name: The Sun
short_description: A G-type main-sequence star and the gravitational anchor of the Solar System, providing the light and heat that make life on Earth possible.

layers.name: Core
layers.description: The dense center where nuclear fusion converts hydrogen into helium, releasing the energy that powers the Sun.

layers.name: Radiative Zone
layers.description: Energy from the core slowly migrates outward as radiation, a journey that can take hundreds of thousands of years.

layers.name: Convective Zone
layers.description: Hot plasma rises and cooler plasma sinks in convection currents, carrying energy toward the surface.

layers.name: Photosphere
layers.description: The visible 'surface' of the Sun, where light escapes into space. Home to sunspots.

layers.name: Chromosphere
layers.description: A thin layer above the photosphere, visible as a reddish glow during solar eclipses.

layers.name: Corona
layers.description: The Sun's outer atmosphere, visible during total eclipses and far hotter than the surface below it — a phenomenon still studied by scientists.

phenomena.name: Sunspots
phenomena.description: Cooler, darker regions on the photosphere caused by concentrated magnetic field activity.

phenomena.name: Solar Flares
phenomena.description: Sudden, intense bursts of radiation released from the Sun's surface.

phenomena.name: Prominences
phenomena.description: Large, bright loops of plasma extending outward from the Sun's surface, shaped by magnetic fields.

phenomena.name: Solar Wind
phenomena.description: A continuous stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun through the Solar System.

phenomena.name: Nuclear Fusion
phenomena.description: In the core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium under immense pressure and temperature, releasing the energy that lets the Sun shine.

facts: The Sun accounts for about 99.8% of the total mass of the Solar System.
Light from the Sun takes approximately 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.
The Sun is roughly 4.6 billion years old and is expected to shine for billions more years.
The Sun's corona is far hotter than its visible surface, a puzzle known as the 'coronal heating problem'.
Around one million Earths could fit inside the volume of the Sun.
